lessons.title: Exercise 1.1 — Powers of i, Basic Operations, Conjugate and Modulus
lessons.notes_html:
The Imaginary Unit and Powers of i

A complex number is written as z = a + ib or as the ordered pair (a, b), where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part. The imaginary unit i = sqrt(-1) satisfies:

i^2 = -1

The powers of i repeat in a cycle of 4:

Poweri^1i^2i^3i^4
Valuei-1-i1

To evaluate a higher power, remove multiples of 4 from the exponent. Also (-i)^2 = -1 and (-i)^4 = 1. Within 1 <= n <= 4, i^n equals i when n = 1, -1 when n = 2, -i when n = 3 and 1 when n = 4, and i^n + i^(n+1) + i^(n+2) + i^(n+3) = 0 for all n in Z.

Operations on Complex Numbers

Addition and subtraction are done by grouping the real parts together and the imaginary parts together. Multiplication is done term by term, replacing i^2 by -1. For ordered pairs:

(a, b)(c, d) = (ac - bd, ad + bc)

Division is done by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, because (c + di)(c - di) = c^2 + d^2 is real. Powers are simplified by first finding the square, for example (1 + i)^2 = 2i, and then multiplying on.

Conjugate, Absolute Value and the Complex Plane

The conjugate of z = a + ib is z-bar = a - ib: only the sign of the imaginary part is reversed. The absolute value (modulus) is:

|z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)

On the complex plane (Argand diagram) the real part is measured along the horizontal real axis and the imaginary part along the vertical imaginary axis. The point (a, b) represents z, and the length of the vector from the origin to that point is |z|. To solve a complex equation, write both sides in a + ib form and equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

Worked Example: Powers of i

Example: Evaluate i^10 . (-i^12)

Step 1: Recall the cycle of powers of i: i^1 = i, i^2 = -1, i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1, and the pattern repeats every 4

Step 2: Write i^10 = i^8 x i^2 = (i^4)^2 x i^2

Step 3: Substitute i^4 = 1 and i^2 = -1, so i^10 = 1 x (-1) = -1

Step 4: Write i^12 = (i^4)^3 = 1^3 = 1, so -i^12 = -1

Step 5: Multiply the two values, (-1) x (-1) = 1. Final answer: 1

Worked Example: Division of Two Complex Numbers

Example: Simplify (7 + 4i) / (8 + 5i)

Step 1: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, (8 - 5i)

Step 2: Expand the numerator, (7 + 4i)(8 - 5i) = 56 - 35i + 32i - 20i^2 = 56 - 3i + 20 = 76 - 3i, using i^2 = -1

Step 3: Expand the denominator, (8 + 5i)(8 - 5i) = 64 + 25 = 89

Step 4: Divide both parts by 89. Final answer: 76/89 - (3/89)i

Worked Example: Conjugate and Absolute Value

Example: Find the conjugate and absolute value of sqrt(7) - 3i

Step 1: Here a = sqrt(7) and b = -3

Step 2: The conjugate reverses the sign of the imaginary part, giving sqrt(7) + 3i

Step 3: The absolute value is |z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) = sqrt(7 + 9)

Step 4: Simplify, sqrt(16) = 4. Final answer: Conjugate = sqrt(7) + 3i, absolute value = 4

mcqs.q: What is the value of i^10 . (-i^12)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 1. i^10 = (i^4)^2 x i^2 = 1 x (-1) = -1, and i^12 = (i^4)^3 = 1 so -i^12 = -1. Multiplying gives (-1) x (-1) = 1.

mcqs.q: What is the value of (-i)^16 . (-i)^6?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is -1. Since (-i)^4 = 1, (-i)^16 = 1, and (-i)^6 = (-i)^4 x (-i)^2 = 1 x (-1) = -1. The product is 1 x (-1) = -1.

mcqs.q: For any integer n, what is i^n + i^(n+1) + i^(n+2) + i^(n+3)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0. Taking i^n common leaves 1 + i + i^2 + i^3 = 1 + i - 1 - i = 0, so the whole expression is i^n x 0 = 0 for every integer n.

mcqs.q: Using (a, b)(c, d) = (ac - bd, ad + bc), what is (-6, 3) . (4, -2)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (-18, 24). The first component is (-6)(4) - (3)(-2) = -24 + 6 = -18, and the second is (-6)(-2) + (3)(4) = 12 + 12 = 24.

mcqs.q: What is (2, 3) / (4, 5) as an ordered pair?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (23/41, 2/41). Multiply (2 + 3i)/(4 + 5i) by (4 - 5i): the numerator is 8 + 2i + 15 = 23 + 2i and the denominator is 16 + 25 = 41.

mcqs.q: What is (4 + 5i)(6 + 7i)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is -11 + 58i. Expanding gives 24 + 28i + 30i + 35i^2 = 24 + 58i - 35 = -11 + 58i, using i^2 = -1.

mcqs.q: What is (1 + i)^3?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is -2 + 2i. First (1 + i)^2 = 1 + 2i + i^2 = 2i, then 2i(1 + i) = 2i + 2i^2 = 2i - 2 = -2 + 2i.

mcqs.q: What is (7 + 4i) / (8 + 5i)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 76/89 - (3/89)i. Multiplying top and bottom by (8 - 5i) gives numerator (7 + 4i)(8 - 5i) = 76 - 3i and denominator 64 + 25 = 89.

mcqs.q: What are the conjugate and absolute value of sqrt(7) - 3i?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is: conjugate sqrt(7) + 3i and absolute value 4. The conjugate reverses the sign of the imaginary part, and |z| = sqrt(7 + 9) = sqrt(16) = 4.

mcqs.q: What is the length of the vector representing -5 + 2i on the complex plane?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is sqrt(29). The length of the vector is the modulus |z| = sqrt((-5)^2 + 2^2) = sqrt(25 + 4) = sqrt(29).

lessons.title: Exercise 1.2 — Properties of Complex Numbers, Inverses and Triangle Inequality
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Addition and Multiplication

Complex numbers follow the same laws as real numbers. With z1 = 3 - 4i, z2 = 4 + 5i and z3 = -5 + 6i, this exercise verifies each law by computing both sides separately:

  • Commutative: z1 + z2 = z2 + z1 and z1 z2 = z2 z1
  • Associative: (z1 + z2) + z3 = z1 + (z2 + z3) and (z1 z2) z3 = z1 (z2 z3)
  • Distributive: z1 (z2 + z3) = z1 z2 + z1 z3

Conjugate and Modulus Properties

For z = a + ib with conjugate z-bar = a - ib:

z + z-bar = 2a (real) and z - z-bar = 2ib (imaginary)

|z1 . z2| = |z1| |z2| and |z1/z2| = |z1|/|z2|

Also |z| = |-z| = |z-bar| = |-z-bar|, (z-bar)-bar = z, z z-bar = |z|^2, and the conjugate of a sum, product or quotient is the sum, product or quotient of the conjugates. The Triangle inequality states:

|z1| - |z2| <= |z1 + z2| <= |z1| + |z2|

Additive and Multiplicative Inverses

The additive inverse of z = a + ib is -a - ib: every sign is reversed, and z plus its additive inverse gives the additive identity (0, 0). The multiplicative inverse is:

1/z = (a/(a^2 + b^2), -b/(a^2 + b^2))

By definition, the additive inverse (c, d) satisfies (a, b) + (c, d) = (0, 0), and the multiplicative inverse satisfies (a, b)(c, d) = (1, 0), which gives two equations for c and d. A negative power means a reciprocal: z^(-1) = 1/z and z^(-2) = 1/z^2, after which the real and imaginary parts are read off from the a + ib form.

Worked Example: Commutative Law for Addition

Example: Let z1 = 3 - 4i and z2 = 4 + 5i. Verify that addition of complex numbers is commutative

Step 1: Commutative property for addition means z1 + z2 = z2 + z1, so we compute both sides separately

Step 2: Left side, z1 + z2 = (3 - 4i) + (4 + 5i)

Step 3: Add the real parts, 3 + 4 = 7, and add the imaginary parts, -4i + 5i = i, so the left side is 7 + i

Step 4: Right side, z2 + z1 = (4 + 5i) + (3 - 4i)

Step 5: Add the real parts, 4 + 3 = 7, and add the imaginary parts, 5i - 4i = i, so the right side is 7 + i

Step 6: Both sides are equal, so addition is commutative for these numbers. Final answer: z1 + z2 = z2 + z1 = 7 + i, hence verified

Worked Example: Multiplicative Inverse

Example: Find the multiplicative inverse of 3 + 5i

Step 1: The multiplicative inverse of z = a + ib is (a/(a^2 + b^2), -b/(a^2 + b^2))

Step 2: Here a = 3 and b = 5, so a^2 + b^2 = 9 + 25 = 34

Step 3: The first component is 3/34

Step 4: The second component is -5/34

Step 5: Check: (3 + 5i)(3/34 - (5/34)i) = (9 + 25)/34 = 1. Final answer: (3/34, -5/34), that is 3/34 - (5/34)i

Worked Example: Real and Imaginary Parts of a Negative Power

Example: Find real and imaginary parts of (sqrt(2) + i)^(-2)

Step 1: The power -2 means the reciprocal of the square, so first find (sqrt(2) + i)^2 = 2 + 2 sqrt(2) i + i^2 = 1 + 2 sqrt(2) i

Step 2: Now take the reciprocal, (sqrt(2) + i)^(-2) = 1/(1 + 2 sqrt(2) i)

Step 3: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate (1 - 2 sqrt(2) i)

Step 4: The numerator becomes 1 - 2 sqrt(2) i

Step 5: The denominator becomes 1 + 8 = 9, since (1)^2 + (2 sqrt(2))^2 = 1 + 8

Step 6: Divide, giving 1/9 - (2 sqrt(2)/9) i. Final answer: Real part = 1/9, imaginary part = -2 sqrt(2)/9

mcqs.q: For z1 = 3 - 4i and z2 = 4 + 5i, what is z1 + z2, verifying commutativity of addition?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 7 + i. Adding real parts gives 3 + 4 = 7 and adding imaginary parts gives -4i + 5i = i; computing z2 + z1 gives the same 7 + i.

mcqs.q: For z1 = 3 - 4i and z2 = 4 + 5i, what is z1 z2?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 32 - i. Expanding, (3 - 4i)(4 + 5i) = 12 + 15i - 16i - 20i^2 = 12 - i + 20 = 32 - i, using i^2 = -1.

mcqs.q: With z1 = 3 - 4i, z2 = 4 + 5i and z3 = -5 + 6i, what is (z1 + z2) + z3?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2 + 7i. First z1 + z2 = 7 + i, then (7 + i) + (-5 + 6i) = 2 + 7i, which also equals z1 + (z2 + z3) by associativity.

mcqs.q: With z1 = 3 - 4i, z2 = 4 + 5i and z3 = -5 + 6i, what is z1(z2 + z3) by the distributive law?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 41 + 37i. First z2 + z3 = -1 + 11i, then (3 - 4i)(-1 + 11i) = -3 + 33i + 4i - 44i^2 = -3 + 37i + 44 = 41 + 37i.

mcqs.q: If z = a + ib, what is z + z-bar?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2a. Since z-bar = a - ib, adding gives (a + ib) + (a - ib) = 2a, and the imaginary parts cancel, so the result is purely real.

mcqs.q: What is the additive inverse of 6 - 5i?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is -6 + 5i. The additive inverse reverses every sign, and indeed (6 - 5i) + (-6 + 5i) = 0, the additive identity.

mcqs.q: What is the multiplicative inverse of 3 + 5i?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 3/34 - (5/34)i. Using 1/z = (a/(a^2 + b^2), -b/(a^2 + b^2)) with a = 3, b = 5 gives a^2 + b^2 = 34, so the inverse is (3/34, -5/34).

mcqs.q: What is the multiplicative inverse of the ordered pair (12, -7)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (12/193, 7/193). Here a^2 + b^2 = 144 + 49 = 193, so the inverse is (a/193, -b/193) = (12/193, 7/193) because b = -7.

mcqs.q: What are the real and imaginary parts of (sqrt(2) + i)^(-2)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is real part 1/9 and imaginary part -2 sqrt(2)/9. First (sqrt(2) + i)^2 = 1 + 2 sqrt(2) i, and 1/(1 + 2 sqrt(2) i) = (1 - 2 sqrt(2) i)/9 after multiplying by the conjugate.

mcqs.q: Which statement is the triangle inequality for complex numbers z1 and z2?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is |z1| - |z2| <= |z1 + z2| <= |z1| + |z2|. This is the triangle inequality stated in the notes: the modulus of a sum lies between the difference and the sum of the moduli.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.3 — Simultaneous Equations, Linear Factors and Completing the Square
lessons.notes_html:
Simultaneous Equations with Complex Coefficients

Two linear equations in w and z are solved by elimination or substitution. Multiply one equation by a suitable complex number so one unknown cancels, solve for the other, then substitute back. Useful facts: (2 - i)(2 + i) = 5 and 1/i = -i.

Polynomials as Products of Linear Factors

A sum of squares becomes a difference of squares by using i^2 = -1, since (9bi)^2 = -81b^2:

z^2 + 81b^2 = z^2 - (9bi)^2 = (z - 9bi)(z + 9bi)

For a cubic, find one integer root by the factor theorem, trying factors of the constant term. Divide by that factor using synthetic division to get a quadratic, then solve it with the quadratic formula. Each root r gives a linear factor (z - r):

z = [-b +- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)]/(2a)

Solving Quadratics by Completing the Square

Move the constant to the right, add the square of half the coefficient of z to both sides, and factor the left side as a perfect square. Then take the square root of both sides, using sqrt(-1) = i and both signs.

Worked Example: Simultaneous Equations

Example: Solve 3z + (2 + i)w = 11 - i, (2 - i)z - w = -1 + i for w and z

Step 1: Write the equations as (1) 3z + (2 + i)w = 11 - i and (2) (2 - i)z - w = -1 + i

Step 2: To eliminate w, multiply equation (2) by (2 + i): (2 - i)(2 + i)z - (2 + i)w = (-1 + i)(2 + i)

Step 3: Simplify the left coefficient, (2 - i)(2 + i) = 4 + 1 = 5

Step 4: Simplify the right side, (-1 + i)(2 + i) = -2 - i + 2i + i^2 = -3 + i, so the new equation is 5z - (2 + i)w = -3 + i

Step 5: Add this to equation (1) to cancel the w terms, 3z + 5z = (11 - i) + (-3 + i), giving 8z = 8, so z = 1

Step 6: Substitute z = 1 in equation (2), (2 - i) - w = -1 + i

Step 7: Solve for w, w = (2 - i) - (-1 + i) = 2 - i + 1 - i = 3 - 2i

Step 8: Check in equation (1): 3(1) + (2 + i)(3 - 2i) = 3 + (6 - 4i + 3i - 2i^2) = 3 + 8 - i = 11 - i, which is correct. Final answer: z = 1, w = 3 - 2i

Worked Example: Product of Linear Factors

Example: Write z^3 + 3z^2 + z - 5 as the product of linear factors

Step 1: Try integer roots among the factors of 5, namely 1, -1, 5, -5, using the factor theorem

Step 2: Put z = 1: 1 + 3 + 1 - 5 = 0, so (z - 1) is a factor

Step 3: Divide by (z - 1) by synthetic division with coefficients 1, 3, 1, -5: bring down 1, multiply by 1 and add successively to get the quotient coefficients 1, 4, 5 with remainder 0

Step 4: So the polynomial is (z - 1)(z^2 + 4z + 5)

Step 5: Solve z^2 + 4z + 5 = 0 by the quadratic formula, z = [-4 +- sqrt(16 - 20)]/2 = [-4 +- sqrt(-4)]/2 = [-4 +- 2i]/2 = -2 +- i

Step 6: So the quadratic gives the factors (z + 2 - i) and (z + 2 + i)

Step 7: Collect all three linear factors. Final answer: z^3 + 3z^2 + z - 5 = (z - 1)(z + 2 - i)(z + 2 + i)

Worked Example: Completing the Square

Example: Solve z^2 - 4z + 5 = 0 by completing the squares, where z is a complex number

Step 1: Move the constant to the right side, z^2 - 4z = -5

Step 2: Half of the coefficient of z is -2, and its square is 4; add 4 to both sides, z^2 - 4z + 4 = -5 + 4

Step 3: Factor the left side as a perfect square, (z - 2)^2 = -1

Step 4: Take the square root of both sides, z - 2 = +- sqrt(-1) = +- i

Step 5: Add 2 to both sides, z = 2 +- i. Final answer: z = 2 + i or z = 2 - i

mcqs.q: Solving 3z + (2 + i)w = 11 - i and (2 - i)z - w = -1 + i gives which values?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is z = 1, w = 3 - 2i. Multiplying the second equation by (2 + i) gives 5z - (2 + i)w = -3 + i; adding the first equation gives 8z = 8, so z = 1, and back-substitution gives w = 3 - 2i.

mcqs.q: What is 1/i?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is -i. Multiply numerator and denominator by i: 1/i = i/i^2 = i/(-1) = -i, which is the useful fact listed in the notes for this exercise.

mcqs.q: What is (2 - i)(2 + i)?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 5. The product is a difference of squares type: (2 - i)(2 + i) = 4 - i^2 = 4 + 1 = 5, since i^2 = -1.

mcqs.q: Written as a product of linear factors, z^2 + 81b^2 equals what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (z - 9bi)(z + 9bi). Since (9bi)^2 = 81b^2 i^2 = -81b^2, we have z^2 + 81b^2 = z^2 - (9bi)^2, a difference of squares.

mcqs.q: Written as a product of linear factors, 4z^2 + 9b^2 equals what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (2z - 3bi)(2z + 3bi). Because (3bi)^2 = 9b^2 i^2 = -9b^2, the sum 4z^2 + 9b^2 = (2z)^2 - (3bi)^2 factorises as a difference of squares.

mcqs.q: What is z^3 + 3z^2 + z - 5 as a product of linear factors?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (z - 1)(z + 2 - i)(z + 2 + i). z = 1 is a root since 1 + 3 + 1 - 5 = 0; dividing gives z^2 + 4z + 5, whose roots by the quadratic formula are -2 + i and -2 - i.

mcqs.q: What is z^3 + 3z^2 + 4z + 2 as a product of linear factors?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (z + 1)(z + 1 - i)(z + 1 + i). z = -1 is a root since -1 + 3 - 4 + 2 = 0; the remaining quadratic factor gives the conjugate roots -1 + i and -1 - i.

mcqs.q: Solving z^2 - 4z + 5 = 0 by completing the square gives what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is z = 2 + i or z = 2 - i. Completing the square gives (z - 2)^2 = -1, so z - 2 = +- i and therefore z = 2 +- i.

mcqs.q: What is z^3 - 7z^2 + 19z - 13 as a product of linear factors?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (z - 1)(z - 3 - 2i)(z - 3 + 2i). z = 1 is a root since 1 - 7 + 19 - 13 = 0, and the quadratic factor that remains has the conjugate roots 3 + 2i and 3 - 2i.

mcqs.q: The quadratic z^2 + 4z + 5 = 0, obtained when factorising in this exercise, has which roots?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is -2 + i and -2 - i. By the quadratic formula, z = [-4 +- sqrt(16 - 20)]/2 = [-4 +- sqrt(-4)]/2 = [-4 +- 2i]/2 = -2 +- i.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.1 — Types of Matrices, Transpose, Equality and Special Matrices
lessons.notes_html:
Matrix, Order and Elements

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers. If it has m rows and n columns, its order is m x n. The element in row i and column j is written aij. A = [aij] is the short form; writing out every aij is the tabular (expanded) form.

Main Types of Matrices

  • Row matrix: only one row, order 1 x n.
  • Column matrix: only one column, order m x 1.
  • Square matrix: rows = columns.
  • Diagonal matrix: square, every off-diagonal element is 0; written diag(d1, d2, ...).
  • Scalar matrix: diagonal, all diagonal elements equal to one scalar.
  • Identity (unit) matrix I: scalar matrix with diagonal elements all 1.
  • Upper / lower triangular: square, all elements below / above the main diagonal are 0.

Transpose, Symmetric and Skew-Symmetric

The transpose A^t is found by interchanging rows and columns; an m x n matrix gives an n x m transpose.

A^t = A means A is symmetric; A^t = -A means A is skew-symmetric

In a skew-symmetric matrix every main diagonal element must be 0.

Hermitian and Skew-Hermitian

Abar is the conjugate of A. A is Hermitian if (Abar)^t = A, and skew-Hermitian if (Abar)^t = -A. Hermitian: real diagonal elements and aij = conjugate of aji. Skew-Hermitian: diagonal elements zero or purely imaginary.

Equality of Matrices

Two matrices are equal only when they have the same order and every pair of corresponding elements is equal. Unknowns are found by equating corresponding elements.

Special Square Matrices

  • Nilpotent: A^p = 0 for some smallest positive p, called the index.
  • Periodic: A^(k+1) = A for the smallest positive k, called the period; period 1 means A^2 = A.
  • Idempotent: A^2 = A.
  • Involutory: A^2 = I.

Worked Example: Type of a Diagonal Matrix

Example: Specify the type of the matrix [sqrt(5), 0, 0; 0, -1/3, 0; 0, 0, 2/5].

Step 1: Count the rows and columns: the matrix has 3 rows and 3 columns, so it is a square matrix of order 3.

Step 2: Look at the off-diagonal elements: every element with i not equal to j is 0, for example a12 = 0, a23 = 0 and a31 = 0.

Step 3: Look at the main diagonal elements: sqrt(5), -1/3 and 2/5 are non-zero but they are not all equal, so it is not a scalar matrix and not an identity matrix.

Step 4: A square matrix whose off-diagonal elements are all zero is called a diagonal matrix, and it is also both upper triangular and lower triangular.

Step 5: Final answer: It is a square diagonal matrix of order 3, written as diag(sqrt(5), -1/3, 2/5).

Worked Example: Unknowns from Equality of Matrices

Example: Find the unknowns from [x + y, 0, z; 9, 2x + y, 6; a, 1, 3] = [3, 0, 3x; 9, 4, 6; y, 1, 3].

Step 1: Equate corresponding elements: the (1,1) elements give x + y = 3 ...(A).

Step 2: The (1,3) elements give z = 3x ...(B).

Step 3: The (2,2) elements give 2x + y = 4 ...(C), and the (3,1) elements give a = y ...(D); all other positions agree automatically.

Step 4: Subtract (A) from (C): (2x + y) - (x + y) = 4 - 3, so x = 1.

Step 5: Put x = 1 in (A): 1 + y = 3, so y = 2.

Step 6: Put x = 1 in (B): z = 3(1) = 3, and from (D) a = y = 2.

Step 7: Final answer: x = 1, y = 2, z = 3, a = 2.

mcqs.q: The matrix [sqrt(5), 0, 0; 0, -1/3, 0; 0, 0, 2/5] is best described as what?
options: A diagonal matrix of order 3, diag(sqrt(5), -1/3, 2/5)
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a diagonal matrix of order 3, diag(sqrt(5), -1/3, 2/5). It is square with every off-diagonal element 0, but the diagonal entries are not all equal, so it is neither scalar nor identity.

mcqs.q: The matrix [sqrt(3); 4/7] is which type and order?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a column matrix of order 2 x 1. It has two rows but only one column, which is exactly the definition of a column matrix given in the notes.

mcqs.q: The matrix [i/2, 0, i/3] is which type and order?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a row matrix of order 1 x 3. It has only one row and three columns, matching the definition of a row matrix in the notes.

mcqs.q: A scalar matrix whose diagonal elements are all 1 is called what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the identity (unit) matrix I. The notes define I as the scalar matrix with every diagonal element equal to 1, for example I4 of order 4 in the exercise.

mcqs.q: The matrix [sqrt(7), 0, 0; 0, sqrt(7), 0; 0, 0, sqrt(7)] is which type?
options: A diagonal matrix but not scalar
A scalar matrix with scalar sqrt(7)
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a scalar matrix with scalar sqrt(7). It is diagonal and all three diagonal elements are equal to the same scalar sqrt(7), but they are not 1, so it is not the identity.

mcqs.q: What is the transpose of [-8, 7; 3, 0]?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is [-8, 3; 7, 0]. The transpose interchanges rows and columns, so the first row [-8, 7] becomes the first column and the second row [3, 0] becomes the second column.

mcqs.q: The matrix [7, 5, 8; 5, -1, 6; 8, 6, -1] is which type?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is symmetric, because A^t = A. Each entry equals its mirror entry across the diagonal: a12 = a21 = 5, a13 = a31 = 8 and a23 = a32 = 6, and the diagonal is not all zero, so it cannot be skew-symmetric.

mcqs.q: The matrix [0, -5, -6; 5, 0, 7; 6, -7, 0] is which type?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is skew-symmetric. Its transpose is its negative, A^t = -A: for example a12 = -5 while a21 = 5, and every main diagonal element is 0, as a skew-symmetric matrix requires.
The correct answer is x = 1, y = 2, z = 3, a = 2. Equating elements gives x + y = 3 and 2x + y = 4, so subtracting gives x = 1 and then y = 2; also z = 3x = 3 and a = y = 2.

mcqs.q: A square matrix A is Hermitian when which condition holds?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (Abar)^t = A. The notes define a Hermitian matrix by this condition, with real diagonal elements and aij equal to the conjugate of aji; (Abar)^t = -A is the skew-Hermitian condition.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.2 — Addition, Subtraction, Scalar Multiplication and Matrix Multiplication
lessons.notes_html:
Addition and Subtraction

Two matrices can be added or subtracted only when they have the same order. Add or subtract corresponding elements, position by position. Addition is commutative: A + B = B + A.

Scalar Multiplication and Combinations

To multiply a matrix by a scalar such as 2 or 3, multiply every element by that scalar. Combinations such as 2A - B or 3A + B + I are built by first scaling, then adding or subtracting entry by entry. Adding I changes only the diagonal elements.

Matrix Multiplication — Conformability

The product AB exists only when the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. If A is m x n and B is n x p, then AB is m x p. If the inner numbers do not match, the product is not possible. Each element of the product is a row of A multiplied by a column of B: add the products of corresponding entries.

(AB)^t = B^t A^t

Multiplication is not commutative in general, and the cancellation law does not hold: XY = XZ does not force Y = Z. A matrix polynomial such as A^2 - 5A + 4I is evaluated by computing each term and then adding entry by entry.

Worked Example: Addition of Complex Matrices

Example: If A = [1 + i, 2, 3i; 4i, 5 - i, 2 + 3i; 0, 5, 1 - i] and B = [2 + i, 3 - i, 4; i, 0, 5 - i; 6 + i, 2, 2 + 3i], find A + B.

Step 1: Both matrices are 3 x 3, so they can be added entry by entry.

Step 2: First row: (1 + i) + (2 + i) = 3 + 2i, 2 + (3 - i) = 5 - i, 3i + 4 = 4 + 3i.

Step 3: Second row: 4i + i = 5i, (5 - i) + 0 = 5 - i, (2 + 3i) + (5 - i) = 7 + 2i.

Step 4: Third row: 0 + (6 + i) = 6 + i, 5 + 2 = 7, (1 - i) + (2 + 3i) = 3 + 2i.

Step 5: Final answer: A + B = [3 + 2i, 5 - i, 4 + 3i; 5i, 5 - i, 7 + 2i; 6 + i, 7, 3 + 2i].

Worked Example: A Product That Is Not Possible

Example: Let A = [3, -4, 1; 4, 5, 7; -2, -3, 8] (3 x 3) and B = [3, 4, -1; 2, -3, 5] (2 x 3). Wherever possible compute AB.

Step 1: A is 3 x 3 and B is 2 x 3.

Step 2: For the product AB the number of columns of A must equal the number of rows of B, but A has 3 columns while B has only 2 rows.

Step 3: The inner numbers 3 and 2 do not match, so the multiplication cannot be performed.

Step 4: Final answer: AB is not possible (the matrices are not conformable for multiplication in this order).

Worked Example: Matrix Multiplication AC

Example: With A as above and C = [-5, 4; 6, -3; -2, 7], compute AC.

Step 1: Check the orders: A is 3 x 3 and C is 3 x 2; the inner numbers 3 and 3 match, so AC exists and has order 3 x 2.

Step 2: First row of AC: (3)(-5) + (-4)(6) + (1)(-2) = -15 - 24 - 2 = -41, and (3)(4) + (-4)(-3) + (1)(7) = 12 + 12 + 7 = 31.

Step 3: Second row: (4)(-5) + (5)(6) + (7)(-2) = -20 + 30 - 14 = -4, and (4)(4) + (5)(-3) + (7)(7) = 16 - 15 + 49 = 50.

Step 4: Third row: (-2)(-5) + (-3)(6) + (8)(-2) = 10 - 18 - 16 = -24, and (-2)(4) + (-3)(-3) + (8)(7) = -8 + 9 + 56 = 57.

Step 5: Final answer: AC = [-41, 31; -4, 50; -24, 57].

mcqs.q: For A and B of Exercise 2.2 Q1 (both 3 x 3 complex matrices), what is the (2, 3) entry of A + B?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 7 + 2i. The (2, 3) entries are 2 + 3i in A and 5 - i in B, and adding corresponding entries gives (2 + 3i) + (5 - i) = 7 + 2i.

mcqs.q: For the same A and B, what is the (1, 1) entry of A - B?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is -1. The (1, 1) entries are 1 + i in A and 2 + i in B, so subtracting corresponding entries gives (1 + i) - (2 + i) = -1.

mcqs.q: For the same A and B, what is the (1, 1) entry of 2A - B?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is i. Doubling A gives (1, 1) entry 2 + 2i, and subtracting the (1, 1) entry of B gives (2 + 2i) - (2 + i) = i.

mcqs.q: With A of order 3 x 3 and B of order 2 x 3, why is the product AB not possible?
options: Because A is square and B is not
Because B has more columns than A
Because the columns of A (3) do not equal the rows of B (2)
Because both matrices must have the same order
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the columns of A (3) do not equal the rows of B (2). The product AB exists only when the inner numbers match, and here 3 is not equal to 2, so the matrices are not conformable in this order.

mcqs.q: With A = [3, -4, 1; 4, 5, 7; -2, -3, 8] and C = [-5, 4; 6, -3; -2, 7], what is the first row of AC?
For the same A and C, what is the (2, 2) entry of AC?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 50. Multiply the second row of A by the second column of C: (4)(4) + (5)(-3) + (7)(7) = 16 - 15 + 49 = 50.

mcqs.q: With B of order 2 x 3 and A of order 3 x 3, what is the order of the product BA?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2 x 3. The inner numbers 3 and 3 match, and the product takes the outer numbers: rows of B (2) by columns of A (3), giving order 2 x 3.

mcqs.q: Which identity for the transpose of a product is stated in the notes?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (AB)^t = B^t A^t. The notes state this reversal rule, and Exercise 2.2 verifies it numerically: (AB)^t and B^t A^t both equal [40, 17, -2; -4, 32, -4; 31, 29, -27] for the given matrices.
The correct answer is 17. The (1, 1) entry of A^2 is (-2)(-2) + (1)(-1) + 0 = 3, so the result is 3 - 5(-2) + 4 = 3 + 10 + 4 = 17, matching the book answer [17, -3, 3; 3, 23, 12; -8, 32, 28].

lessons.title: Exercise 2.3 — Determinants, Singular Matrices, Adjoint and Inverse of a Matrix
lessons.notes_html:
Determinant of a 3 x 3 Matrix

Only square matrices have determinants. Expanding along the first row, each element is multiplied by its 2 x 2 minor Mij, with signs + - + across the row:

det = a11 M11 - a12 M12 + a13 M13

For a 2 x 2 matrix [a, b; c, d], the determinant is ad - bc. The determinant of a diagonal or triangular matrix is the product of its main diagonal elements. A common factor of a whole row or column can be taken outside the determinant.

Singular and Non-Singular Matrices

A is singular if det A = 0; A is non-singular if det A is not 0

If one row is a constant multiple of another row, the determinant is 0. To find x making a matrix singular, set its determinant equal to 0 and solve.

Minor, Cofactor and Adjoint

The minor Mij is the 2 x 2 determinant left after deleting row i and column j. The cofactor carries the sign:

Aij = (-1)^(i+j) Mij

The adjoint, adj A, is the transpose of the cofactor matrix. For a 2 x 2 matrix, adj A is found by swapping the diagonal entries and changing the signs of the off-diagonal entries.

Inverse by the Adjoint Method

A^-1 = (1 / det A) x adj A, provided det A is not 0

Useful identities verified in this exercise: (A^-1)^-1 = A, (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1, adj(AB) = (adj B)(adj A), and (5A)^-1 = (1/5) A^-1.

Worked Example: Evaluating a Determinant

Example: Evaluate the determinant |5, 4, 3; 3, -4, 0; 2, 3, 1|.

Step 1: Expand along the first row: det = 5 x M11 - 4 x M12 + 3 x M13, where the M are the 2 x 2 minors.

Step 2: M11 = (-4)(1) - (0)(3) = -4, so the first term is 5 x (-4) = -20.

Step 3: M12 = (3)(1) - (0)(2) = 3, so the second term is -4 x 3 = -12.

Step 4: M13 = (3)(3) - (-4)(2) = 9 + 8 = 17, so the third term is 3 x 17 = 51.

Step 5: Add the three terms: -20 - 12 + 51 = 19.

Step 6: Final answer: The determinant is 19.

Worked Example: Value of x for a Singular Matrix

Example: Find the value of x for which the matrix [10, 5; 6, x] is singular.

Step 1: The matrix is singular exactly when its determinant is 0.

Step 2: For a 2 x 2 matrix the determinant is (10)(x) - (5)(6) = 10x - 30.

Step 3: Set the determinant equal to zero: 10x - 30 = 0.

Step 4: Solve: 10x = 30, so x = 3.

Step 5: Final answer: x = 3.

Worked Example: Inverse by the Adjoint Method

Example: Use the adjoint method to calculate the inverse of [5, 6; 3, 4], if possible.

Step 1: Compute the determinant: det = (5)(4) - (6)(3) = 20 - 18 = 2, which is not zero, so the inverse exists.

Step 2: Find the adjoint by swapping the diagonal entries and changing the signs of the off-diagonal entries: adj A = [4, -6; -3, 5].

Step 3: Apply A^-1 = (1/det A) x adj A = (1/2) x [4, -6; -3, 5].

Step 4: Final answer: A^-1 = [2, -3; -3/2, 5/2].

mcqs.q: What is the determinant |5, 4, 3; 3, -4, 0; 2, 3, 1|?
What is the determinant of the 2 x 2 matrix [5, 6; 3, 4]?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2. For a 2 x 2 matrix [a, b; c, d] the determinant is ad - bc, so here it is (5)(4) - (6)(3) = 20 - 18 = 2, which is not zero, so the inverse exists.

mcqs.q: What is the determinant |-2, 4, 3; 5, 4, -2; 2, 7, 3|?
For which value of x is the matrix [10, 5; 6, x] singular?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is x = 3. A matrix is singular when its determinant is 0: (10)(x) - (5)(6) = 10x - 30 = 0, so 10x = 30 and x = 3.

mcqs.q: For which value of x is the matrix [5, 4; x, 8] singular?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is x = 10. Setting the determinant to zero gives (5)(8) - (4)(x) = 40 - 4x = 0, so 4x = 40 and x = 10.

mcqs.q: What is the adjoint of the matrix [3, 4; -1, 2]?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is adj A = [2, -4; 1, 3]. For a 2 x 2 matrix, swap the diagonal entries (giving 2 and 3) and change the signs of the off-diagonal entries (giving -4 and 1).

mcqs.q: Using the adjoint method, what is the inverse of [5, 6; 3, 4]?
What is the determinant of the diagonal matrix [4, 0, 0; 0, 3, 0; 0, 0, 2], and is it singular?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 24, and it is non-singular. The determinant of a diagonal matrix is the product of its diagonal elements, 4 x 3 x 2 = 24, which is not zero, so the matrix is non-singular.

mcqs.q: The cofactor Aij of an element aij is given by which formula?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is Aij = (-1)^(i+j) Mij. The notes define the cofactor as the minor Mij (the determinant left after deleting row i and column j) carrying the sign (-1)^(i+j).

mcqs.q: Which inverse identity is verified in this exercise?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1. The order reverses for a product, and the exercise verifies (AB)^-1 = B^-1 A^-1 = [26/75, -43/75; -17/75, 31/75] for the given A and B; note (5A)^-1 = (1/5) A^-1, not 5 A^-1.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.4 — Properties of Determinants and Proofs Without Expansion
lessons.notes_html:
Properties of Determinants Used in Proofs

  • Property 1: |A| = |A^t| — a determinant equals the determinant of its transpose.
  • Property 3: two identical rows or columns make the determinant 0.
  • Property 5: a common factor of a row or column can be taken outside.
  • Property 6: if every entry of a column is a sum, the determinant splits into a sum of determinants.
  • Property 7: two proportional rows or columns make the determinant 0.
  • Property 8 type operations: adding a multiple of one row (or column) to another does not change the determinant; interchanging two rows or columns changes its sign.

The method of this exercise is: use row and column operations to create two identical or two proportional rows or columns, or to factor out a common factor, and finish with the matching property — all without expanding.

Worked Example: |A| = |A^t|

Example: Let A = [2, 5, 0; 3, 4, 6; 1, -5, 1]. Verify that |A| = |A^t|.

Step 1: Expand |A| along the first row: the minors are M11 = (4)(1) - (6)(-5) = 34, M12 = (3)(1) - (6)(1) = -3, M13 = (3)(-5) - (4)(1) = -19.

Step 2: |A| = 2(34) - 5(-3) + 0(-19) = 68 + 15 + 0 = 83.

Step 3: Write the transpose: A^t = [2, 3, 1; 5, 4, -5; 0, 6, 1].

Step 4: Expand |A^t| along its first row: the minors are (4)(1) - (-5)(6) = 34, (5)(1) - (-5)(0) = 5, (5)(6) - (4)(0) = 30.

Step 5: |A^t| = 2(34) - 3(5) + 1(30) = 68 - 15 + 30 = 83.

Step 6: Both determinants come out the same, as Property 1 states.

Step 7: Final answer: |A| = |A^t| = 83, hence verified.

Worked Example: Proof Without Expanding — Identical Rows

Example: Without expanding, prove that |x + y, y + z, z + x; z, x, y; 1, 1, 1| = 0.

Step 1: Apply the row operation R1 -> R1 + R2, which does not change the value of a determinant (Property 8 type operation).

Step 2: The new first row is (x + y + z), (y + z + x), (z + x + y), that is, every entry becomes x + y + z.

Step 3: Take the common factor (x + y + z) out of the first row (Property 5): the first row becomes 1, 1, 1.

Step 4: The first row is now identical to the third row 1, 1, 1.

Step 5: By Property 3, a determinant with two identical rows is zero.

Step 6: Final answer: The determinant is 0, hence proved without expansion.

Worked Example: Proof Without Expanding — Proportional Rows

Example: Without expanding, prove that |x + 1, x + 3, x + 5; x + 4, x + 6, x + 8; x + 7, x + 9, x + 11| = 0.

Step 1: Notice the pattern: each row increases by 3 down the columns and each column increases down the rows in steps of 3.

Step 2: Apply R2 -> R2 - R1: the second row becomes (3, 3, 3).

Step 3: Apply R3 -> R3 - R1: the third row becomes (6, 6, 6).

Step 4: The third row is now exactly 2 times the second row, so two rows are proportional.

Step 5: By Property 7, the determinant is zero.

Step 6: Final answer: The determinant is 0, hence proved.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is |A| = |A^t| = 83. Expanding, |A| = 2(34) - 5(-3) + 0(-19) = 83, and expanding the transpose gives 2(34) - 3(5) + 1(30) = 83, verifying Property 1.

mcqs.q: Property 1 of determinants states which equality?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is |A| = |A^t|. Property 1 says a determinant equals the determinant of its transpose, which the exercise verifies with the value 83 on both sides.

mcqs.q: What is the value of a determinant that has two identical rows?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0. Property 3 states that two identical rows or columns make the determinant 0; the worked proof makes the first row identical to the third row 1, 1, 1 and finishes with this property.

mcqs.q: What is the value of a determinant that has two proportional rows?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 0. Property 7 states that two proportional rows or columns make the determinant 0; in the worked proof the rows (3, 3, 3) and (6, 6, 6) are proportional with factor 2.

mcqs.q: In the proof that |x + y, y + z, z + x; z, x, y; 1, 1, 1| = 0, after R1 -> R1 + R2 the common factor taken out of the first row is what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is x + y + z. After R1 -> R1 + R2 every first-row entry becomes x + y + z; taking this factor out (Property 5) leaves the row 1, 1, 1, identical to the third row, so the determinant is 0 by Property 3.

mcqs.q: What happens to a determinant when two rows are interchanged?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it changes sign. This is one of the Property 8 type operations listed in the notes, unlike adding a multiple of one row to another, which leaves the value unchanged.

mcqs.q: What happens to a determinant when a multiple of one row is added to another row?
options: It is multiplied by that multiple
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that it does not change. This Property 8 type operation is the main tool of the exercise: operations such as R2 -> R2 - R1 and R1 -> R1 + R2 are used freely in proofs without expanding.

mcqs.q: In the proof for |x + 1, x + 3, x + 5; x + 4, x + 6, x + 8; x + 7, x + 9, x + 11|, applying R2 -> R2 - R1 and R3 -> R3 - R1 gives which rows?
options: (6, 6, 6) and (3, 3, 3) as second and third rows
(3, 3, 3) and (6, 6, 6) as second and third rows
mcqs.why: The correct answer is second row (3, 3, 3) and third row (6, 6, 6). Each entry of R2 exceeds R1 by 3 and each entry of R3 exceeds R1 by 6; the third row is 2 times the second, so the rows are proportional and the determinant is 0 by Property 7.

mcqs.q: Property 5 of determinants allows what?
options: Taking a common factor of a whole row or column outside the determinant
Splitting a column sum into two determinants
mcqs.why: The correct answer is taking a common factor of a whole row or column outside the determinant. Property 5 is used in the worked proof to factor (x + y + z) out of the first row; splitting a sum is Property 6 instead.

mcqs.q: Property 6 of determinants states what happens if every entry of a column is a sum?
options: The determinant splits into a sum of determinants
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the determinant splits into a sum of determinants. Property 6, as listed in the notes, lets a determinant whose column entries are sums be written as a sum of two determinants.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.5 — Echelon Form, Reduced Echelon Form, Rank and Inverse by Row Operations
lessons.notes_html:
Elementary Row Operations

  • Interchange two rows: Ri <-> Rj.
  • Multiply a row by a non-zero number: Ri -> k Ri.
  • Add a multiple of one row to another: Ri -> Ri + k Rj.

Echelon and Reduced Echelon Form

In echelon form, every leading entry is 1, each leading 1 lies to the right of the one above it, entries below a leading entry are 0, and any zero row sits at the bottom. In reduced echelon form, entries above each leading 1 are also cleared to 0, so each pivot column contains only its leading 1.

Rank of a Matrix

Rank = number of non-zero rows in the echelon form

A 3 x 3 matrix with rank 3 has a non-zero determinant; if a zero row appears, its determinant is 0.

Inverse by Row Operations

Write the augmented matrix [A : I] and apply row operations until the left side becomes I. The right side is then A^-1. If a zero row appears on the left, the inverse does not exist.

Worked Example: Echelon Form

Example: Reduce [5, 9, 3; -3, 5, 6; -1, -5, -3] into echelon form using elementary row operations.

Step 1: Start with A = [5, 9, 3; -3, 5, 6; -1, -5, -3]; bring the simplest row to the top: R1 <-> R3 gives [-1, -5, -3; -3, 5, 6; 5, 9, 3].

Step 2: R1 -> (-1) R1 gives [1, 5, 3; -3, 5, 6; 5, 9, 3], so the first leading entry is 1.

Step 3: R2 -> R2 + 3R1 gives [1, 5, 3; 0, 20, 15; 5, 9, 3], clearing the entry below the first pivot.

Step 4: R3 -> R3 - 5R1 gives [1, 5, 3; 0, 20, 15; 0, -16, -12].

Step 5: R2 -> (1/20) R2 gives [1, 5, 3; 0, 1, 3/4; 0, -16, -12], making the second leading entry 1.

Step 6: R3 -> R3 + 16R2 gives [1, 5, 3; 0, 1, 3/4; 0, 0, 0].

Step 7: The result has leading 1s moving to the right, zeros below each leading entry, and the zero row at the bottom, which is exactly echelon form.

Step 8: Final answer: The echelon form is [1, 5, 3; 0, 1, 3/4; 0, 0, 0].

Worked Example: Rank of a Matrix

Example: Find the rank of [1, 2, 3; 2, 3, 4; 0, 2, 2] using elementary row operations.

Step 1: The rank is the number of non-zero rows in the echelon form, so reduce the matrix.

Step 2: R2 -> R2 - 2R1 gives [1, 2, 3; 0, -1, -2; 0, 2, 2].

Step 3: R2 -> (-1) R2 gives [1, 2, 3; 0, 1, 2; 0, 2, 2].

Step 4: R3 -> R3 - 2R2 gives [1, 2, 3; 0, 1, 2; 0, 0, -2].

Step 5: R3 -> (-1/2) R3 gives [1, 2, 3; 0, 1, 2; 0, 0, 1], an echelon form with no zero row.

Step 6: There are 3 non-zero rows (this agrees with det A = 2, which is not zero).

Step 7: Final answer: The rank of the matrix is 3.

mcqs.q: Reducing [5, 9, 3; -3, 5, 6; -1, -5, -3] to echelon form gives which last row?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is [0, 0, 0]. The reduction ends with echelon form [1, 5, 3; 0, 1, 3/4; 0, 0, 0]: leading 1s move to the right, entries below them are 0, and the zero row sits at the bottom.

mcqs.q: What is the rank of [1, 2, 3; 2, 3, 4; 0, 2, 2]?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 3. Its echelon form [1, 2, 3; 0, 1, 2; 0, 0, 1] has 3 non-zero rows, and the rank is the number of non-zero rows in echelon form; this agrees with det A = 2, not zero.

mcqs.q: What is the rank of [2, 3, 4; 3, 1, 2; -1, 2, 2]?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is 2. Reducing this matrix of Exercise 2.5 by elementary row operations leaves only 2 non-zero rows in its echelon form, and the rank is defined as that number of non-zero rows.

mcqs.q: Reducing [1, 2, -1; 2, 4, 1; 3, 6, 2] to echelon form gives what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is [1, 2, -1; 0, 0, 1; 0, 0, 0]. This is the echelon form given in the book for this matrix: leading 1s move to the right, entries below each leading 1 are 0, and the zero row is at the bottom.

mcqs.q: The reduced echelon form of [3, 5, 4; 4, 1, 5; 7, 6, 3] is what?
options: Its echelon form with a zero row
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the identity matrix. The book gives the reduced echelon form of this full-rank matrix as [1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1], with entries above each leading 1 also cleared to 0.

mcqs.q: The rank of a matrix is defined as what?
options: The number of rows of the matrix
The number of non-zero rows in its echelon form
The number of columns of the matrix
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the number of non-zero rows in its echelon form. The notes define rank this way, so a 3 x 3 matrix whose echelon form has a zero row has rank less than 3 and determinant 0.

mcqs.q: In the elementary operation Ri -> k Ri, what condition must k satisfy?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that k must be non-zero. The notes list the operation as multiplying a row by a non-zero number; multiplying by 0 would destroy the row and is not an allowed elementary operation.

mcqs.q: To find A^-1 by row operations, the augmented matrix [A : I] is reduced until what happens?
options: The left side becomes I, and the right side is then A^-1
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the left side becomes I, and the right side is then A^-1. The notes describe exactly this method: apply row operations to [A : I] until the left side is I, and read the inverse from the right side.

mcqs.q: During inverse by row operations, if a zero row appears on the left side, what follows?
options: The inverse is the zero matrix
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that the inverse does not exist. The notes state this directly: a zero row on the left of [A : I] means the left side can never become I, so A has no inverse.

mcqs.q: Which feature belongs to reduced echelon form but not to plain echelon form?
options: Zero rows sit at the bottom
Entries above each leading 1 are also 0
mcqs.why: The correct answer is that entries above each leading 1 are also 0. The notes state that in reduced echelon form each pivot column contains only its leading 1, while plain echelon form only clears the entries below each leading 1.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.6 — Solving Linear Systems: Homogeneous, Inversion, Gauss, Gauss-Jordan and Cramer
lessons.notes_html:
Systems of Linear Equations

A system is written as AX = B. It is homogeneous when B = 0 (AX = 0) and non-homogeneous otherwise. The augmented matrix Ab joins B as an extra column. Missing terms are entered as 0.

Homogeneous Systems

AX = 0 always has the trivial solution x = y = z = 0. Non-trivial solutions exist exactly when rank(A) is less than the number of unknowns. Then one unknown is free: set it equal to k and express the others in terms of k.

Consistency of a Non-Homogeneous System

Consistent if rank(A) = rank(Ab); inconsistent if rank(A) is less than rank(Ab)

If the common rank also equals the number of unknowns, the solution is unique.

Four Solving Methods

  • Matrix inversion: X = A^-1 B, usable only when det A is not 0.
  • Gauss elimination: reduce Ab to echelon form, then back-substitute from the last row upwards.
  • Gauss-Jordan: reduce Ab all the way to reduced echelon form; the solution is read off directly.
  • Cramer's rule: x = |A1| / |A|, y = |A2| / |A|, z = |A3| / |A|, where Ai is A with column i replaced by B; usable only when |A| is not 0.

Worked Example: Homogeneous System, Non-Trivial Solutions

Example: Solve x + 2y - 2z = 0, 2x + y + 5z = 0, 5x + 4y + 8z = 0 for non-trivial solutions, if possible.

Step 1: Write the system as AX = 0 with A = [1, 2, -2; 2, 1, 5; 5, 4, 8]; a homogeneous system has non-trivial solutions exactly when rank(A) is less than the number of unknowns, 3.

Step 2: R2 -> R2 - 2R1 gives [1, 2, -2; 0, -3, 9; 5, 4, 8].

Step 3: R3 -> R3 - 5R1 gives [1, 2, -2; 0, -3, 9; 0, -6, 18].

Step 4: R3 -> R3 - 2R2 gives [1, 2, -2; 0, -3, 9; 0, 0, 0]; R2 -> (-1/3) R2 gives the echelon form [1, 2, -2; 0, 1, -3; 0, 0, 0], so rank(A) = 2, less than 3, and non-trivial solutions exist.

Step 5: The reduced system is x + 2y - 2z = 0 and y - 3z = 0, that is y = 3z.

Step 6: Put y = 3z in the first equation: x + 6z - 2z = 0, so x = -4z.

Step 7: Take z as the free variable, z = k, where k is any non-zero real number for a non-trivial solution.

Step 8: Final answer: The non-trivial solutions are x = -4k, y = 3k, z = k for k not equal to 0; for example k = 1 gives (x, y, z) = (-4, 3, 1).

Worked Example: Cramer's Rule

Example: Solve x - 2y + z = 2, 2x + 2y - z = 4, x + y = 0 using Cramer's Rule.

Step 1: The coefficient matrix is A = [1, -2, 1; 2, 2, -1; 1, 1, 0] and B = [2; 4; 0]; compute |A| by expanding along the first row: |A| = 1[(2)(0) - (-1)(1)] - (-2)[(2)(0) - (-1)(1)] + 1[(2)(1) - (2)(1)] = 1(1) + 2(1) + 1(0) = 3, not zero, so Cramer's rule applies.

Step 2: Replace the first column by B: |A1| = |2, -2, 1; 4, 2, -1; 0, 1, 0| = 2[(2)(0) - (-1)(1)] - (-2)[(4)(0) - (-1)(0)] + 1[(4)(1) - (2)(0)] = 2(1) + 2(0) + 4 = 6.

Step 3: Replace the second column by B: |A2| = |1, 2, 1; 2, 4, -1; 1, 0, 0|; expanding along the third row gives 1 x [(2)(-1) - (1)(4)] = -6 (the other two terms contain the factor 0).

Step 4: Replace the third column by B: |A3| = |1, -2, 2; 2, 2, 4; 1, 1, 0| = 1[(2)(0) - (4)(1)] - (-2)[(2)(0) - (4)(1)] + 2[(2)(1) - (2)(1)] = -4 - 8 + 0 = -12.

Step 5: Apply Cramer's rule: x = |A1| / |A| = 6/3 = 2, y = |A2| / |A| = -6/3 = -2, z = |A3| / |A| = -12/3 = -4.

Step 6: Final answer: x = 2, y = -2, z = -4.

mcqs.q: A system AX = B is called homogeneous when what holds?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is B = 0. The notes define a homogeneous system by AX = 0, that is B = 0, and a non-homogeneous system otherwise; the augmented matrix Ab joins B as an extra column.

mcqs.q: The homogeneous system AX = 0 always has which solution?
options: The trivial solution x = y = z = 0
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the trivial solution x = y = z = 0. The notes state that AX = 0 always has this solution, and non-trivial solutions exist exactly when rank(A) is less than the number of unknowns.

mcqs.q: For x + 2y - 2z = 0, 2x + y + 5z = 0, 5x + 4y + 8z = 0, the non-trivial solutions are what?
options: x = -4k, y = 3k, z = k for k not 0
x = 4k, y = 3k, z = k for k not 0
x = -4k, y = -3k, z = k for k not 0
mcqs.why: The correct answer is x = -4k, y = 3k, z = k for k not 0. The echelon form has rank 2, less than 3 unknowns, with y - 3z = 0 giving y = 3z, and then x + 6z - 2z = 0 giving x = -4z; setting z = k gives the family.

mcqs.q: For the homogeneous system of Exercise 2.6 Q1(ii), the non-trivial solutions are what?
options: x = k, y = k, z = k
x = 2k, y = -k, z = k for k not 0
mcqs.why: The correct answer is x = 2k, y = -k, z = k for k not 0. This is the solution family given in the book for that system, with z = k as the free variable and x and y expressed in terms of k.

mcqs.q: A non-homogeneous system is consistent exactly when what holds?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is rank(A) = rank(Ab). The notes state the system is consistent if the two ranks are equal and inconsistent if rank(A) is less than rank(Ab); if the common rank also equals the number of unknowns, the solution is unique.

mcqs.q: When does a consistent non-homogeneous system have a unique solution?
options: When rank(A) is less than the number of unknowns
When the common rank equals the number of unknowns
mcqs.why: The correct answer is when the common rank equals the number of unknowns. The notes state this condition directly: consistency needs rank(A) = rank(Ab), and uniqueness needs that common rank to equal the number of unknowns.

mcqs.q: The matrix inversion method writes the solution of AX = B as what, and when can it be used?
options: X = A^-1 B, only when det A is not 0
X = A B, only when det A = 0
X = A^-1 B, only when det A = 0
mcqs.why: The correct answer is X = A^-1 B, usable only when det A is not 0. The notes give this formula for the inversion method, and A^-1 exists only for a non-singular matrix, that is when det A is not 0.

mcqs.q: Solving x - 2y + z = 2, 2x + 2y - z = 4, x + y = 0 by Cramer's rule gives x = what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is x = 2. Here |A| = 3 and |A1| = 6 (first column replaced by B), so Cramer's rule gives x = |A1|/|A| = 6/3 = 2; the full solution is x = 2, y = -2, z = -4.

mcqs.q: Solving x + 2y + z = 8, 2x - y + z = 3, x + y - z = 0 by the matrix inversion method gives what?
mcqs.why: The correct answer is x = 1, y = 2, z = 3. Here det A = 9, not zero, so X = A^-1 B = (1/9)[9; 18; 27] = [1; 2; 3], and it checks: 1 + 4 + 3 = 8, 2 - 2 + 3 = 3 and 1 + 2 - 3 = 0.

mcqs.q: In Gauss elimination, after reducing the augmented matrix Ab to echelon form, how is the solution found?
options: By reading it off directly with no substitution
By back-substitution from the last row upwards
By replacing columns of A with B
By taking determinants of A and Ab
mcqs.why: The correct answer is by back-substitution from the last row upwards. The notes distinguish Gauss elimination (echelon form, then back-substitute) from Gauss-Jordan, which reduces all the way to reduced echelon form so the solution is read off directly.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.1 — Scalars, Vectors and Position Vectors in the Plane
lessons.notes_html:
Scalar and Vector Quantities

A scalar needs only magnitude. A vector needs magnitude and direction to be specified completely.

Vectors: force, velocity, acceleration, weight

Scalars: speed, area, work, volume, mass

Vector Between Two Points

For points P and Q, subtract the coordinates of the initial point P from the coordinates of the terminal point Q, component by component.

PQ = (position vector of Q) - (position vector of P)

Magnitude and Unit Vector

For p = xi + yj, the magnitude is found from the components, and a unit vector in the direction of p is p divided by its magnitude.

|p| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2), unit vector = p / |p|

Two vectors are equal only when their corresponding components are equal.

Section Formula

For internal division of AB in the ratio m:n, where a and b are the position vectors of A and B:

r = (m x b + n x a) / (m + n)

Worked Example: Vector PQ in Component Form

Example: Write the vector PQ in the form xi + yj, where P(4, 6) and Q(-4, 5).

Step 1: Use the rule PQ = (position vector of Q) - (position vector of P), that is subtract the coordinates of the initial point from the coordinates of the terminal point.

Step 2: The x-component is x = -4 - 4 = -8.

Step 3: The y-component is y = 5 - 6 = -1.

Step 4: Write the components with the unit vectors i and j: PQ = -8i - 1j.

Step 5: Final answer: PQ = -8i - j.

Worked Example: Linear Combination of Vectors

Example: If p = -5i + 4j, q = -3i + 5j and r = -6i + 7j, find 3p + 5q - 4r.

Step 1: Multiply p by 3: 3p = -15i + 12j.

Step 2: Multiply q by 5: 5q = -15i + 25j.

Step 3: Multiply r by -4: -4r = -4(-6i + 7j) = 24i - 28j.

Step 4: Add the i-components: -15 - 15 + 24 = -6.

Step 5: Add the j-components: 12 + 25 - 28 = 9.

Step 6: Combine: 3p + 5q - 4r = -6i + 9j.

Step 7: Final answer: 3p + 5q - 4r = -6i + 9j.

Worked Example: Unit Vector

Example: Find the unit vector in the direction of p = -3i + 8j.

Step 1: A unit vector in the direction of p is p / |p|, so first find the magnitude.

Step 2: |p| = sqrt((-3)^2 + (8)^2) = sqrt(9 + 64) = sqrt(73).

Step 3: Divide each component of p by sqrt(73): the i-component is -3/sqrt(73) and the j-component is 8/sqrt(73).

Step 4: Write the result as a single vector: (-3i + 8j)/sqrt(73), whose magnitude is sqrt(9 + 64)/sqrt(73) = 1, as a unit vector must have.

Step 5: Final answer: The unit vector is (-3i + 8j)/sqrt(73).

Worked Example: Dividing a Join in a Ratio

Example: Find the position vector of the point dividing the join of A and B in the ratio 3:5, where the position vectors of A and B are 4i - 5j and 2i + 7j respectively.

Step 1: For internal division in the ratio m:n, the position vector is r = (m x b + n x a)/(m + n), where a and b are the position vectors of A and B; here m = 3 and n = 5.

Step 2: Compute m x b = 3(2i + 7j) = 6i + 21j.

Step 3: Compute n x a = 5(4i - 5j) = 20i - 25j.

Step 4: Add them: (6 + 20)i + (21 - 25)j = 26i - 4j.

Step 5: Divide by m + n = 8: r = (26/8)i - (4/8)j = (13/4)i - (1/2)j.

Step 6: Final answer: The position vector is (13/4)i - (1/2)j.

mcqs.q: Which statement about force is correct?
options: Force is a scalar because it is measured only in newtons
Force is a vector because magnitude and direction are both needed to specify it
Force is a scalar because it has no direction
Force is neither a scalar nor a vector
mcqs.why: Force is a vector: a push of 10 N is incomplete until its direction is also given, so both magnitude and direction are needed.

mcqs.q: Which of the following quantities is a scalar?
mcqs.why: Mass is a scalar: a value such as 10 kg completely describes it and no direction can be attached to it, unlike velocity, acceleration and weight.

mcqs.q: For P(4, 6) and Q(-4, 5), the vector PQ in the form xi + yj is
mcqs.why: PQ is Q minus P: x = -4 - 4 = -8 and y = 5 - 6 = -1, so PQ = -8i - j.

mcqs.q: For P(-3, 6) and Q(5, 9), the vector PQ is
mcqs.why: PQ is Q minus P: x = 5 - (-3) = 8 and y = 9 - 6 = 3, so PQ = 8i + 3j.

mcqs.q: If p = -5i + 4j, q = -3i + 5j and r = -6i + 7j, then 3p + 5q - 4r equals
mcqs.why: 3p + 5q - 4r is the correct answer: 3p = -15i + 12j, 5q = -15i + 25j and -4r = 24i - 28j; adding gives i: -15 - 15 + 24 = -6 and j: 12 + 25 - 28 = 9.

mcqs.q: If p = -5i + 4j and q = -3i + 5j, then 2p + 3q equals
The unit vector in the direction of p = -3i + 8j is
mcqs.why: The unit vector is (-3i + 8j)/sqrt(73): |p| = sqrt(9 + 64) = sqrt(73), and dividing p by its magnitude gives a vector of length 1.

mcqs.q: If (5, 7) = (5, -q), then q equals
mcqs.why: q = -7 is correct: equal vectors have equal corresponding components, so 7 = -q, and multiplying by -1 gives q = -7.

mcqs.q: The vector in the direction of a = 2i - 3j having magnitude 6 units is
mcqs.why: The required vector is (12i - 18j)/sqrt(13): |a| = sqrt(4 + 9) = sqrt(13), the unit vector is (2i - 3j)/sqrt(13), and multiplying by 6 gives the answer.

mcqs.q: The position vector of the point dividing AB internally in the ratio 3:5, where A has position vector 4i - 5j and B has position vector 2i + 7j, is
mcqs.why: Using r = (3b + 5a)/8: 3(2i + 7j) + 5(4i - 5j) = 26i - 4j, and dividing by 8 gives (13/4)i - (1/2)j.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.2 — Vectors in Three Dimensions
lessons.notes_html:
Vectors in Three Dimensions

A vector in space is written as a1i + a2j + a3k, or as a column vector with three entries. A missing component is 0, for example v = 3i - 5j means v = 3i - 5j + 0k.

|a| = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2 + a3^2)

Addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication are done component by component. Scalar multiplication multiplies every component by the scalar; a negative scalar also reverses the direction.

Vector Between Two Points

A1A2 = (coordinates of A2) - (coordinates of A1)

|c w| = |c| |w|

Unit Vector and a Vector of Given Length

a-hat = a / |a|

For the opposite direction, use the negative. Also a = |a| x (a-hat).

Section Formula in Space

Internal division in the ratio m:n uses r = (m x (second position vector) + n x (first position vector))/(m + n). External division uses r = (m x (second position vector) - n x (first position vector))/(m - n). A midpoint is the average of the position vectors of its endpoints.

Worked Example: Linear Combination in Space

Example: Let u = i + 2j + k, v = 3i - 5j and w = -8i + 7j - 2k. Find 3u + 2v.

Step 1: Note that v = 3i - 5j means v = 3i - 5j + 0k, so all three components are available.

Step 2: Multiply u by 3 component-wise: 3u = 3i + 6j + 3k.

Step 3: Multiply v by 2 component-wise: 2v = 6i - 10j + 0k.

Step 4: Add the i-components: 3 + 6 = 9; add the j-components: 6 - 10 = -4; add the k-components: 3 + 0 = 3.

Step 5: Combine: 3u + 2v = 9i - 4j + 3k.

Step 6: Final answer: 3u + 2v = 9i - 4j + 3k.

Worked Example: Magnitude of a Sum

Example: Let u = i - 3j + 2k, v = i + j and w = 2i + 2j - 4k. Find |u + v - w|.

Step 1: Write v with all components: v = 1i + 1j + 0k.

Step 2: Add the i-components of u + v - w: 1 + 1 - 2 = 0.

Step 3: Add the j-components: -3 + 1 - 2 = -4.

Step 4: Add the k-components: 2 + 0 - (-4) = 6.

Step 5: So u + v - w = 0i - 4j + 6k = -4j + 6k.

Step 6: Find its magnitude: |u + v - w| = sqrt(0^2 + (-4)^2 + (6)^2) = sqrt(0 + 16 + 36) = sqrt(52) = 2sqrt(13).

Step 7: Final answer: |u + v - w| = 2sqrt(13).

Worked Example: Vector Between Two Points in Space

Example: Find the vector A1A2 when A1(5, -2, 1) and A2(2, 4, 2).

Step 1: The vector A1A2 is (coordinates of A2) - (coordinates of A1), component by component.

Step 2: x-component: 2 - 5 = -3.

Step 3: y-component: 4 - (-2) = 6.

Step 4: z-component: 2 - 1 = 1.

Step 5: Combine: A1A2 = -3i + 6j + k.

Step 6: Final answer: A1A2 = -3i + 6j + k.

Worked Example: Vector of Given Magnitude in a Given Direction

Example: Find the vector OA, where |OA| = 6 and OA is in the direction of the vector (2, -3, 6).

Step 1: OA is a scalar multiple of the given direction vector: OA = |OA| x (unit vector in that direction).

Step 2: The magnitude of the direction vector (2, -3, 6) is sqrt((2)^2 + (-3)^2 + (6)^2) = sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = sqrt(49) = 7.

Step 3: The unit vector in that direction is (2i - 3j + 6k)/7.

Step 4: Multiply by the required magnitude 6: OA = 6(2i - 3j + 6k)/7 = (12i - 18j + 36k)/7.

Step 5: Check: |OA| = (6/7) x 7 = 6, as required.

Step 6: Final answer: OA = (12/7)i - (18/7)j + (36/7)k.

mcqs.q: In three dimensions, the vector v = 3i - 5j written with all three components is
mcqs.why: v = 3i - 5j + 0k is correct: a missing component in three dimensions is 0, so the k-component of 3i - 5j is 0.

mcqs.q: Let u = i + 2j + k and v = 3i - 5j. Then 3u + 2v equals
Let u = i + 2j + k and v = 3i - 5j. Then v - 2u equals
If a = -5i + 3j - 4k, then -2a equals
mcqs.why: -2a = 10i - 6j + 8k: multiplying every component by -2 gives -2 x (-5) = 10, -2 x 3 = -6 and -2 x (-4) = 8; the negative scalar also reverses direction.

mcqs.q: If a = -5i + 3j - 4k, then 3|a| equals
mcqs.why: 3|a| = 15sqrt(2): |a| = sqrt(25 + 9 + 16) = sqrt(50) = 5sqrt(2), and multiplying this magnitude by 3 gives 15sqrt(2).

mcqs.q: Let u = i - 3j + 2k, v = i + j and w = 2i + 2j - 4k. Then |u + v - w| equals
mcqs.why: |u + v - w| = 2sqrt(13): u + v - w = -4j + 6k because i: 1 + 1 - 2 = 0, j: -3 + 1 - 2 = -4 and k: 2 + 0 + 4 = 6; the magnitude is sqrt(0 + 16 + 36) = sqrt(52) = 2sqrt(13).

mcqs.q: The vector A1A2 when A1(5, -2, 1) and A2(2, 4, 2) is
The vector OA, where |OA| = 6 and OA is in the direction of the vector (2, -3, 6), is
mcqs.why: OA = (12i - 18j + 36k)/7: the direction vector has magnitude sqrt(4 + 9 + 36) = 7, its unit vector is (2i - 3j + 6k)/7, and multiplying by 6 gives the answer.

mcqs.q: P, Q, R have position vectors (1, 1, -1), (1, -1, 2) and (0, 1, 1). The position vector of the point dividing QR internally in the ratio 3:2 is
mcqs.why: For internal division r = (3R + 2Q)/5: 3(0, 1, 1) + 2(1, -1, 2) = (2, 1, 7), and dividing by 5 gives (2/5, 1/5, 7/5).

mcqs.q: If a = 3i - 5j + 2k and b = -i - 2j + 3k, then |a - b| equals
mcqs.why: |a - b| = sqrt(26): a - b = 4i - 3j - k because i: 3 + 1 = 4, j: -5 + 2 = -3 and k: 2 - 3 = -1; the magnitude is sqrt(16 + 9 + 1) = sqrt(26).

lessons.title: Exercise 3.3 — Laws of Vector Addition and Scalar Multiplication
lessons.notes_html:
Zero Vector and Inverse

The zero vector is 0 = 0i + 0j + 0k.

0 + a = a + 0 = a

The additive inverse changes every sign: a + (-a) = 0.

Commutative and Associative Laws

a + b = b + a

u + (v + w) = (u + v) + w

Scalar Multiplication Laws

m(a) = (a)m

m(n(a)) = (mn)(a)

m(a + b) = ma + mb

(m + n)a = ma + na

Worked Example: Zero Vector as Identity

Example: If a = -5i + 3j - 4k and b = 2i + 4j + 5k, verify that 0 + a = a + 0 = a, where 0 is the zero vector.

Step 1: The zero vector is 0 = 0i + 0j + 0k; vector addition is done component-wise.

Step 2: Compute 0 + a component-wise: i: 0 + (-5) = -5; j: 0 + 3 = 3; k: 0 + (-4) = -4.

Step 3: So 0 + a = -5i + 3j - 4k = a.

Step 4: Compute a + 0 component-wise: i: -5 + 0 = -5; j: 3 + 0 = 3; k: -4 + 0 = -4.

Step 5: So a + 0 = -5i + 3j - 4k = a.

Step 6: Both orders give a itself, which shows 0 behaves as the identity for vector addition.

Step 7: Final answer: 0 + a = a + 0 = a = -5i + 3j - 4k, verified.

Worked Example: Commutative Law of Addition

Example: If a = -5i + 3j - 4k and b = 2i + 4j + 5k, verify the commutative law for vector addition.

Step 1: The commutative law claims a + b = b + a; compute both sides component-wise.

Step 2: a + b, i-components: -5 + 2 = -3.

Step 3: a + b, j-components: 3 + 4 = 7.

Step 4: a + b, k-components: -4 + 5 = 1, so a + b = -3i + 7j + k.

Step 5: b + a, i-components: 2 - 5 = -3; j-components: 4 + 3 = 7; k-components: 5 - 4 = 1, so b + a = -3i + 7j + k.

Step 6: The two sides are identical because ordinary addition of numbers is commutative in each component.

Step 7: Final answer: a + b = b + a = -3i + 7j + k, so the commutative law is verified.

Worked Example: Associative Law of Addition

Example: Let u = 3i + j + 5k, v = i - 2j and w = -i + 3j - k. Verify the associative law of vector addition.

Step 1: The associative law claims u + (v + w) = (u + v) + w; write v with all components: v = 1i - 2j + 0k.

Step 2: Compute v + w: i: 1 - 1 = 0; j: -2 + 3 = 1; k: 0 - 1 = -1, so v + w = 0i + 1j - 1k.

Step 3: Left side: u + (v + w): i: 3 + 0 = 3; j: 1 + 1 = 2; k: 5 - 1 = 4, so u + (v + w) = 3i + 2j + 4k.

Step 4: Compute u + v: i: 3 + 1 = 4; j: 1 - 2 = -1; k: 5 + 0 = 5, so u + v = 4i - j + 5k.

Step 5: Right side: (u + v) + w: i: 4 - 1 = 3; j: -1 + 3 = 2; k: 5 - 1 = 4, so (u + v) + w = 3i + 2j + 4k.

Step 6: The left and right sides are equal.

Step 7: Final answer: u + (v + w) = (u + v) + w = 3i + 2j + 4k, so the associative law is verified.

Worked Example: Distributive Law for a Scalar

Example: Let a = 3i + j + 5k and b = -5i + 3j - 4k be two vectors, and m = 3, n = 7 be scalars. Prove that m(a + b) = ma + mb.

Step 1: First compute a + b component-wise: i: 3 - 5 = -2; j: 1 + 3 = 4; k: 5 - 4 = 1, so a + b = -2i + 4j + k.

Step 2: Left side: m(a + b) = 3(-2i + 4j + k) = -6i + 12j + 3k.

Step 3: Compute ma = 3(3i + j + 5k) = 9i + 3j + 15k.

Step 4: Compute mb = 3(-5i + 3j - 4k) = -15i + 9j - 12k.

Step 5: Right side: ma + mb: i: 9 - 15 = -6; j: 3 + 9 = 12; k: 15 - 12 = 3, so ma + mb = -6i + 12j + 3k.

Step 6: The left side of Step 2 and the right side of Step 5 are identical.

Step 7: Final answer: m(a + b) = ma + mb = -6i + 12j + 3k, hence proved.

mcqs.q: The zero vector in three dimensions is
mcqs.why: The zero vector is 0i + 0j + 0k: every component is 0, and it satisfies 0 + a = a + 0 = a for every vector a.

mcqs.q: If a = -5i + 3j - 4k, then 0 + a equals
mcqs.why: 0 + a = -5i + 3j - 4k, which is a itself: adding 0 to each component leaves -5, 3 and -4 unchanged, so the zero vector is the additive identity.

mcqs.q: The additive inverse of a = -5i + 3j - 4k is
mcqs.why: The additive inverse is 5i - 3j + 4k: the inverse changes every sign, and a + (-a) = (-5 + 5)i + (3 - 3)j + (-4 + 4)k = 0.

mcqs.q: If a = -5i + 3j - 4k and b = 2i + 4j + 5k, the additive inverse of 2a + 3b is
mcqs.why: The inverse is 4i - 18j - 7k: 2a + 3b = (-10 + 6)i + (6 + 12)j + (-8 + 15)k = -4i + 18j + 7k, and changing every sign gives the answer.

mcqs.q: If a = -5i + 3j - 4k and b = 2i + 4j + 5k, then a + b (which also equals b + a) is
mcqs.why: a + b = -3i + 7j + k: i: -5 + 2 = -3, j: 3 + 4 = 7 and k: -4 + 5 = 1; b + a gives the same components, verifying the commutative law.

mcqs.q: Let u = 3i + j + 5k, v = i - 2j and w = -i + 3j - k. Then u + (v + w), which equals (u + v) + w, is
mcqs.why: u + (v + w) = 3i + 2j + 4k: v + w = j - k, so i: 3 + 0 = 3, j: 1 + 1 = 2 and k: 5 - 1 = 4; grouping the other way gives the same result, verifying associativity.

mcqs.q: Let a = 3i + 2j + 5k and m = 5. Then m(a), which equals (a)m, is
mcqs.why: m(a) = 15i + 10j + 25k: multiplying each component by 5 gives 5 x 3 = 15, 5 x 2 = 10 and 5 x 5 = 25, whichever side the scalar is written on.

mcqs.q: Let a = 5i + 2j - 3k, m = 2 and n = 5. Then m(n(a)), which equals (mn)(a), is
mcqs.why: m(n(a)) = 50i + 20j - 30k: n(a) = 25i + 10j - 15k and doubling gives the answer; equally (mn)(a) = 10a multiplies each component by 10.

mcqs.q: Let a = 3i + j + 5k, b = -5i + 3j - 4k and m = 3. Then m(a + b), which equals ma + mb, is
mcqs.why: m(a + b) = -6i + 12j + 3k: a + b = -2i + 4j + k and multiplying by 3 gives the answer; also ma + mb = (9 - 15)i + (3 + 9)j + (15 - 12)k = -6i + 12j + 3k.

mcqs.q: Let a = 3i + j + 5k, m = 3 and n = 7. Then (m + n)a, which equals ma + na, is
mcqs.why: (m + n)a = 30i + 10j + 50k: m + n = 10, so each component is multiplied by 10; also ma + na = (9 + 21)i + (3 + 7)j + (15 + 35)k gives the same vector.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.4 — Dot Product, Angles and Direction Cosines
lessons.notes_html:
Dot Product

The dot product multiplies corresponding components and adds the products. The result is a scalar, a single number with no i, j, k parts.

a.b = a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3

The dot product is commutative and distributive:

a.b = b.a

a.(b + c) = a.b + a.c

Perpendicular Vectors and Angle Between Vectors

Two non-zero vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular) exactly when their dot product is zero.

cos(theta) = (a.b) / (|a||b|)

Direction Cosines and Direction Angles

The direction cosines are the components divided by the magnitude: cos(alpha) = a1/|a|, cos(beta) = a2/|a|, cos(gamma) = a3/|a|, where alpha, beta, gamma are the direction angles.

cos^2(alpha) + cos^2(beta) + cos^2(gamma) = 1

It follows that sin^2(alpha) + sin^2(beta) + sin^2(gamma) = 2.

Work Done and Projection

W = F.d, projection of a along b = (a.b)/|b|

Worked Example: Dot Product

Example: If a = 2i + 3j + 5k, b = i - 2j - 3k and c = 5i + j - k, find a.b.

Step 1: The dot product multiplies corresponding components and adds the products: a.b = a1b1 + a2b2 + a3b3.

Step 2: i-components product: 2 x 1 = 2.

Step 3: j-components product: 3 x (-2) = -6.

Step 4: k-components product: 5 x (-3) = -15.

Step 5: Add the three products term by term: 2 - 6 - 15 = -19.

Step 6: The dot product is a scalar, so the answer is a single number with no i, j, k parts.

Step 7: Final answer: a.b = -19.

Worked Example: Checking for Orthogonal Vectors

Example: Check whether a = 2i - 3j + 2k and b = 5i + 8j + 7k are orthogonal or not.

Step 1: Two non-zero vectors are orthogonal exactly when their dot product is zero.

Step 2: i-term of the dot product: 2 x 5 = 10.

Step 3: j-term: (-3) x 8 = -24.

Step 4: k-term: 2 x 7 = 14.

Step 5: Add term by term: 10 - 24 + 14 = 0.

Step 6: Since the dot product is zero, the angle between the vectors is 90 deg.

Step 7: Final answer: a.b = 0, so a and b are orthogonal (perpendicular).

Worked Example: Angle Between Two Vectors

Example: Find the angle between the vectors i - 2j + 3k and 3i - 2j + k.

Step 1: Use cos(theta) = (a.b)/(|a||b|), so compute the dot product and both magnitudes.

Step 2: Dot product term by term: i: 1 x 3 = 3; j: (-2) x (-2) = 4; k: 3 x 1 = 3; so a.b = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10.

Step 3: |a| = sqrt(1 + 4 + 9) = sqrt(14).

Step 4: |b| = sqrt(9 + 4 + 1) = sqrt(14).

Step 5: cos(theta) = 10/(sqrt(14) x sqrt(14)) = 10/14 = 5/7.

Step 6: theta = cos^-1(5/7), which is approximately 44.4 deg.

Step 7: Final answer: The angle between the vectors is cos^-1(5/7), approximately 44.4 deg.

Worked Example: Work Done by a Force

Example: Find the work done by the force F = 7i + 9j - 11k in moving an object along a straight line from (4, 2, 7) to (6, 4, 9).

Step 1: Work done by a constant force is W = F.d, where d is the displacement vector.

Step 2: Find the displacement: d = (6 - 4)i + (4 - 2)j + (9 - 7)k = 2i + 2j + 2k.

Step 3: Take the dot product term by term: i: 7 x 2 = 14.

Step 4: j: 9 x 2 = 18.

Step 5: k: (-11) x 2 = -22.

Step 6: Add the products: W = 14 + 18 - 22 = 10.

Step 7: Final answer: The work done is 10 Joules (units of work).

mcqs.q: If a = 2i + 3j + 5k and b = i - 2j - 3k, then a . b equals
mcqs.why: a . b = -19: multiply corresponding components and add, 2 x 1 + 3 x (-2) + 5 x (-3) = 2 - 6 - 15 = -19, a scalar with no i, j, k parts.

mcqs.q: If a = 2i + 3j + 5k, b = i - 2j - 3k and c = 5i + j - k, then a . (b + c) equals
mcqs.why: a . (b + c) = -11: b + c = 6i - j - 4k, and the dot product is 2 x 6 + 3 x (-1) + 5 x (-4) = 12 - 3 - 20 = -11.

mcqs.q: The vectors a = 2i - 3j + 2k and b = 5i + 8j + 7k are
mcqs.why: They are orthogonal because a . b = 0: the dot product is 2 x 5 + (-3) x 8 + 2 x 7 = 10 - 24 + 14 = 0, so the angle between them is 90 degrees.

mcqs.q: The vectors a = i + 3j - 4k and b = -2i + j + 3k are
mcqs.why: They are not orthogonal because a . b = -11: the dot product is 1 x (-2) + 3 x 1 + (-4) x 3 = -2 + 3 - 12 = -11, which is not zero.

mcqs.q: The angle between i - 2j + 3k and 3i - 2j + k is approximately
mcqs.why: The angle is about 44.4 degrees: a . b = 3 + 4 + 3 = 10, |a| = |b| = sqrt(14), so cos(theta) = 10/14 = 5/7 and theta = cos^-1(5/7), about 44.4 degrees.

mcqs.q: The angle between 3i + 5j - 3k and i - 4j + k is approximately
mcqs.why: The angle is about 136 degrees: a . b = 3 - 20 - 3 = -20, |a| = sqrt(43) and |b| = sqrt(18), so cos(theta) = -20/sqrt(774), about -0.719, giving an obtuse angle of about 136 degrees.

mcqs.q: For the vector 2i + j - 3k, cos(gamma), where gamma is the direction angle with the z-axis, equals
mcqs.why: cos(gamma) = -3/sqrt(14): the magnitude is sqrt(4 + 1 + 9) = sqrt(14), and a direction cosine is its component divided by the magnitude, here the k-component -3 over sqrt(14).

mcqs.q: If two direction angles of a vector are 45 degrees and 60 degrees, the third direction angle can be
mcqs.why: The third angle is 60 degrees or 120 degrees: cos^2(45) + cos^2(60) = 1/2 + 1/4 = 3/4, so cos^2(gamma) = 1/4, cos(gamma) = 1/2 or -1/2, giving gamma = 60 or 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: The work done by the force F = 7i + 9j - 11k in moving an object from (4, 2, 7) to (6, 4, 9) is
mcqs.why: The work done is 10 Joules: the displacement is d = 2i + 2j + 2k, and W = F . d = 7 x 2 + 9 x 2 + (-11) x 2 = 14 + 18 - 22 = 10.

mcqs.q: If a = 2i + 3j + 2k and b = i + 2j + k, the projection of a along b is
mcqs.why: The projection of a along b is 10/sqrt(6): a . b = 2 + 6 + 2 = 10 and |b| = sqrt(1 + 4 + 1) = sqrt(6), so the projection is (a . b)/|b| = 10/sqrt(6).

lessons.title: Exercise 3.5 — Cross Product, Areas and Moments
lessons.notes_html:
Cross Product

The cross product of a and b is a vector, found by the determinant form. With (a1, a2, a3) and (b1, b2, b3) as the components:

a x b = i(a2b3 - a3b2) - j(a1b3 - a3b1) + k(a1b2 - a2b1)

Reversing the order only changes the sign, and the cross product distributes over addition:

a x b = -(b x a)

a x (b + c) = (a x b) + (a x c)

sin(theta) = |a x b| / (|a||b|)

Unit Vector Perpendicular to Two

A unit vector orthogonal to both is (a x b)/|a x b|; its negative also works.

Areas from the Cross Product

Area of parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b = |a x b|

Area of triangle = (1/2)|AB x AC|

Moment of a Force

The moment about A is M = r x F, where r is the vector from the reference point A to the point of application B. Its magnitude can also be found from |Mo| = |r| |F| sin(theta).

Worked Example: Cross Product

Example: Find a x b and b x a if a = 4i + j + k and b = i + 2j + 3k.

Step 1: Use the determinant form: a x b = i(a2b3 - a3b2) - j(a1b3 - a3b1) + k(a1b2 - a2b1), with (a1, a2, a3) = (4, 1, 1) and (b1, b2, b3) = (1, 2, 3).

Step 2: i-component: a2b3 - a3b2 = (1)(3) - (1)(2) = 3 - 2 = 1.

Step 3: j-component: -(a1b3 - a3b1) = -(4 x 3 - 1 x 1) = -(12 - 1) = -11.

Step 4: k-component: a1b2 - a2b1 = (4)(2) - (1)(1) = 8 - 1 = 7.

Step 5: Combine: a x b = 1i - 11j + 7k.

Step 6: The reverse product only changes the sign: b x a = -(a x b) = -1i + 11j - 7k.

Step 7: Final answer: a x b = i - 11j + 7k and b x a = -i + 11j - 7k.

Worked Example: Unit Vector Orthogonal to Both Vectors

Example: Find a unit vector which is orthogonal to both the vectors a = i - 2j + 3k and b = 3i - 2j + k.

Step 1: A vector orthogonal to both a and b is given by the cross product a x b; a unit vector in that direction is then (a x b)/|a x b|.

Step 2: i-component of a x b: a2b3 - a3b2 = (-2)(1) - (3)(-2) = -2 + 6 = 4.

Step 3: j-component: -(a1b3 - a3b1) = -(1 x 1 - 3 x 3) = -(1 - 9) = 8.

Step 4: k-component: a1b2 - a2b1 = (1)(-2) - (-2)(3) = -2 + 6 = 4.

Step 5: So a x b = 4i + 8j + 4k, and |a x b| = sqrt(16 + 64 + 16) = sqrt(96) = 4sqrt(6).

Step 6: Divide by the magnitude: (4i + 8j + 4k)/(4sqrt(6)) = (i + 2j + k)/sqrt(6).

Step 7: The opposite vector -(i + 2j + k)/sqrt(6) is also a unit vector orthogonal to both, since reversing direction keeps it perpendicular to the same plane.

Step 8: Final answer: A unit vector orthogonal to both is (i + 2j + k)/sqrt(6) (and also its negative).

Worked Example: Area of a Parallelogram

Example: Find the area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are represented by a = 5i - j + 3k and b = i + k.

Step 1: The area of the parallelogram with adjacent sides a and b is |a x b|.

Step 2: Write b with all components: b = 1i + 0j + 1k, so (a1, a2, a3) = (5, -1, 3) and (b1, b2, b3) = (1, 0, 1).

Step 3: i-component of a x b: a2b3 - a3b2 = (-1)(1) - (3)(0) = -1 - 0 = -1.

Step 4: j-component: -(a1b3 - a3b1) = -(5 x 1 - 3 x 1) = -(5 - 3) = -2.

Step 5: k-component: a1b2 - a2b1 = (5)(0) - (-1)(1) = 0 + 1 = 1.

Step 6: So a x b = -i - 2j + k, and the area is |a x b| = sqrt((-1)^2 + (-2)^2 + (1)^2) = sqrt(1 + 4 + 1) = sqrt(6).

Step 7: Final answer: The area of the parallelogram is sqrt(6) square units (approx. 2.45 square units).

mcqs.q: If a = 4i + j + k and b = i + 2j + 3k, then a x b equals
mcqs.why: a x b = i - 11j + 7k: i-component 1 x 3 - 1 x 2 = 1, j-component -(4 x 3 - 1 x 1) = -11, and k-component 4 x 2 - 1 x 1 = 7.

mcqs.q: With a = 4i + j + k and b = i + 2j + 3k, b x a equals
mcqs.why: b x a = -i + 11j - 7k: reversing the order of a cross product only changes its sign, so b x a = -(a x b) = -(i - 11j + 7k).

mcqs.q: If a = -2i + 5j - 3k and b = 3i + 2j + k, then a x b equals
mcqs.why: a x b = 11i - 7j - 19k: i-component 5 x 1 - (-3) x 2 = 11, j-component -((-2) x 1 - (-3) x 3) = -7, and k-component (-2) x 2 - 5 x 3 = -19.

mcqs.q: If a = i - 7j + 7k and b = 3i - 2j + 2k, then a x b equals
mcqs.why: a x b = 19j + 19k: i-component (-7) x 2 - 7 x (-2) = 0, j-component -(1 x 2 - 7 x 3) = 19, and k-component 1 x (-2) - (-7) x 3 = 19.

mcqs.q: A unit vector orthogonal to both a = i - 2j + 3k and b = 3i - 2j + k is
mcqs.why: The unit vector is (i + 2j + k)/sqrt(6): a x b = 4i + 8j + 4k with magnitude sqrt(96) = 4sqrt(6), and dividing gives (4i + 8j + 4k)/(4sqrt(6)) = (i + 2j + k)/sqrt(6).

mcqs.q: The area of the parallelogram whose adjacent sides are a = 5i - j + 3k and b = i + k is
mcqs.why: The area is sqrt(6): a x b = -i - 2j + k from i: (-1)(1) - 3 x 0 = -1, j: -(5 x 1 - 3 x 1) = -2, k: 5 x 0 - (-1)(1) = 1, and |a x b| = sqrt(1 + 4 + 1) = sqrt(6).

mcqs.q: The area of the triangle with vertices A(1, 1, 2), B(2, 3, 5) and C(1, 5, 5) is
mcqs.why: The area is (1/2)sqrt(61): AB = i + 2j + 3k and AC = 4j + 3k, AB x AC = -6i - 3j + 4k with magnitude sqrt(36 + 9 + 16) = sqrt(61), and the triangle area is half of this.

mcqs.q: If a = 2i + j + 7k, b = i - 3j + 5k and c = -i + 5j + k, then a x (b + c), which equals (a x b) + (a x c), is
mcqs.why: a x (b + c) = -8i - 12j + 4k: b + c = 2j + 6k, so i: 1 x 6 - 7 x 2 = -8, j: -(2 x 6 - 7 x 0) = -12 and k: 2 x 2 - 1 x 0 = 4; adding a x b and a x c gives the same vector.

mcqs.q: The moment about A(1, 3, 5) of the force F = i + 2j - k applied at B(3, -2, 5) is
mcqs.why: The moment is M = 5i + 2j + 9k: r = AB = 2i - 5j, and r x F has i: (-5)(-1) - 0 x 2 = 5, j: -(2 x (-1) - 0 x 1) = 2 and k: 2 x 2 - (-5) x 1 = 9.

mcqs.q: A 40 N force is applied at the end of a 0.3 m wrench at an angle of 110 degrees. The magnitude of the moment produced is approximately
mcqs.why: The moment magnitude is about 11.28 Nm: |Mo| = |r| |F| sin(theta) = 0.3 x 40 x sin(110 degrees) = 12 x 0.9397, which is approximately 11.28.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.6 — Scalar Triple Product, Volumes and Coplanarity
lessons.notes_html:
Scalar Triple Product

The scalar triple product a.(b x c), also written [a, b, c], equals the determinant whose rows are the components of a, b and c in order. It is a scalar.

[a, b, c] = a.(b x c)

Volumes

Volume of parallelepiped = absolute value of the scalar triple product of its three edge vectors

Volume of tetrahedron = (1/6) of the absolute scalar triple product of the three edge vectors from one vertex

Coplanar Vectors

Three vectors are coplanar exactly when their scalar triple product is zero, because then the parallelepiped they form has zero volume. They are not coplanar when the scalar triple product is not zero. To find an unknown such as lambda for coplanar vectors, set the determinant equal to zero and solve.

Worked Example: Scalar Triple Product

Example: Find the scalar triple product of the vectors i + 2j + 3k, -i - j + k and i + j + k.

Step 1: The scalar triple product a.(b x c) equals the determinant whose rows are the components of a, b and c in order: rows (1, 2, 3), (-1, -1, 1) and (1, 1, 1).

Step 2: Expand along the first row: 1 x [(-1)(1) - (1)(1)] - 2 x [(-1)(1) - (1)(1)] + 3 x [(-1)(1) - (-1)(1)].

Step 3: Evaluate the first minor: (-1)(1) - (1)(1) = -1 - 1 = -2, giving the term 1 x (-2) = -2.

Step 4: Evaluate the second minor: (-1)(1) - (1)(1) = -2, giving the term -2 x (-2) = +4.

Step 5: Evaluate the third minor: (-1)(1) - (-1)(1) = -1 + 1 = 0, giving the term 3 x 0 = 0.
